Traders reported spot premium quotations for imported cathode and SXEW cathode at US$5060/t, indicating that spot premiums have remained at very low levels. This is primarily due to high stock levels and the negative arbitrage between the SHFE and LME which has widened slightly since our last publication. At current prices, the import loss amounts to RMB3,700/t, up from RMB3,000/t two weeks ago. As a result, activity in the import market has been very subdued. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** **April 2012** www.crugroup.com With the cash-to-three-month-backwardation on the LME reaching US$114/t on 19th April and remaining above the premium for bonded physical stock in Shanghai, arbitrage traders have been re-exporting material from Shanghai bonded warehouses to LME warehouses in neighbouring countries. Nevertheless, cathode inventories in Shanghai bonded warehouses are abundant, with market insiders indicating that current inventories amount to around 600,000t. Imports of cathode were apparently sufficiently high

to compensate for the outflow.  The sizeable import levels may seem somewhat surprising in the light of the unfavourable SHFE/LME arbitrage.  Moreover, market insiders have indicated that the short-term domestic consumption outlook continues to be very bleak.  CRU suggests that much of the material is imported by traders who may be using copper as a financing mechanism to take advantage of arbitrage opportunities in other markets, such as currency exchanges. 

Looking ahead, we expect that the negative SHFE/LME arbitrage will begin to weigh on imports over the coming months.  With this, inventories are expected to drawn down but the lacklustre demand in China indicates that this will be a slow decline.  This could put bring downward pressure on copper prices. 

# China plans to phase out 700,000t of smelting capacity 

According to a statement on the website of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, China plans to eliminate 700,000t/y of copper smelting capacity by the end of 2012.  This is part of a government strategy that aims to curb pollution and improve energy efficiency and also includes phasing out smelting capacity for zinc, lead and aluminum.  Last year, the government announced that as part of the 12<sup>th</sup> 5-year plan (2011-15), 800,000t/y of copper smelting capacity would be phased out during 2011-15.  In 2011, 423,300t/y of copper capacity was eliminated as part of this policy. 

It is not clear exactly which operations the most recent announcement relates to and whether it includes operations beyond the previously announced closures.  However, with respect to the closures announced as part of the 12<sup>th</sup> 5-year plan, we believe that the overall impact on production will be small as most operations that are to be shut down were operating at low levels of utilization.  To the extent that the capacity referred to in the most recent announcement includes these operations, the overall effect on production will also be limited.  Moreover, 3.8Mt/y of copper smelting capacity expansions are planned to start up from 2012 to 2015 and this will more than compensate for the planned shutdowns and total blister output will therefore continue to rise.

# Low inventories at Chinese smelters 

This time last year we were hearing consistent reports that Chinese smelters were abundantly stocked with raw materials and, indeed, participation in the spot concentrates market was extremely low.  In 2012, however, the situation appears to be quite different.  Our data on the RMB value of stocks of unprocessed materials, which includes the value of copper and other material contained in scrap and concentrates, indicates a substantial decrease y- o-y. Tongling, Yunnan and Jiangxi registered declines in the value of raw material stocks

Therefore, we can only draw the conclusion that the absolute volume of stocks has decreased and these low inventory levels correspond to the information we have received from market insiders. Many smelters will need to enter the market to secure supplies of raw material, but the short supply on the spot market is weighing against them. The lack of raw material has pushed down spot treatment and refining charges with reports of deals between miners and traders being settled at terms in the low $20s/2.0¢s. This is putting corresponding downward pressure on merchant-smelter terms and we hear reports that the Chinese smelter purchasing team (CSPT) has had to establish a lower limit of $40.0/4.0¢ amongst its members. Moreover, the negative SHFE/LME arbitrage is also cutting into the profit margins. As mentioned in the previous article, the Chinese government is keen to shut down inefficient smelting and refining operations, but given the current challenging economics and tight supply-demand balance, it may be that government intervention is not the only driver of closures in this sector. # Copper prices recover The daily average LME spot copper prices increased to US$8,356/t on 26th April from US$8,054/t on 16th April. The LME remained in backwardation with the cash-to-three-month backwardation reaching US$96 on 26th April. Furthermore, on 25th April the US Federal Reserve announced that it would keep interest rates low until at least 2014 and also expressed a positive outlook for the US economy and the possibility of further quantitative easing in Q3. However, concerns over the continuing weakness in Chinese demand and the weight of high c

athode stockpiles in SHFE warehouses prevented further gains in prices.  As previously mentioned, market insiders have said that Chinese demand remains weak and macroeconomic data indicates that GDP growth in China decelerated again in Q1.  The SHFE cathode inventory declined by 17,000t over the past two weeks but stocks remained abundant, at 204,762t on 27<sup>th</sup> April.  Despite the bleak market sentiment, prices at the SHFE increased slightly, with the daily average SHFE 3-month and cash price at RMB58,460/t and RMB58,300/t, respectively, on April 27<sup>th</sup> .  Market insiders have said that increased buying from major commodity trading companies has compensated for the weak domestic demand in China and helped to push up prices. 

Going forward, the lacklustre demand outlook in China implies that the recovery in prices is likely to be temporary in the very short term. However, our data suggests that the bottom of the economic slowdown in China is likely to have occurred in Q1 and we anticipate a pick-up in growth in the quarters ahead.  We expect that the macroeconomic upturn will provide support for copper demand and prices.
